=== README.md ===
# text-audit

**An audit-and-fix loop for any human-facing text. It runs the mechanical lints, reads the text as a stranger, and repairs the places where the stranger stops. A [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) skill.**

Point it at a text a person will read: a README, a spec section, a decision page, marketing copy, an article. It runs the free mechanical lints first. Then it hands the text to a fresh reader who knows nothing of its history, and that reader marks every place a stranger stops. You repair those places from the source material, and a new reader reads again. The loop ends when two consecutive reads return nothing that blocks a reader.

---

## Why

The author of a text is the worst reader of it. The author already holds the context the text is missing, so the author reads a meaning a stranger cannot reach. Three examples show the shape:

- a term that was never defined;
- a phrase such as "depends on the upstream state", whose slot stands empty;
- a claim whose ground lives in the author's head.

The text reads fine to the person who wrote it, and it stops a stranger cold.

The repair is a reader who holds none of that context. This skill supplies the stranger. A fresh session reads the words on the page and reports where it stopped. Each stop is marked by whether it blocks a reader or only slows one. You repair the blocking stops from the material the text rests on, and a new stranger reads again. Two clean reads in a row show that the stream of stops has reached zero.

This skill grew inside [live-spec](https://github.com/happysasha18/live-spec), out of a comprehension gate its pipeline held every changed spec section to: a panel of fresh readers found new blocking terms on every pass, and the terms already repaired stayed repaired. It was pulled out into its own repository on 2026-08-18 so any project can run the loop, not only that one.

---

## What it does

1. **The mechanical lints first.** Five lints run before any reader:

   - a term defined at first use;
   - a weak relational word with an unfilled slot;
   - requirement shape, where the text is a spec;
   - style and register;
   - one name per thing.

   A machine settles those cheap classes, so the reader spends attention on the ones no machine knows yet. A host project may declare its own scripts for any of these in `.text-audit/lints.json`; where none is declared, a grep fallback needing no script covers the same ground.
2. **Two fresh cold readers.** The text goes to two sessions with zero context on its history: one under a printed reader-prompt, one under an unprompted brief holding only the text and the task. Both return the places a stranger stops, each marked blocking or non-blocking. Neither fixes anything, and each writes down the guess it made in place of a missing answer.
3. **Fixes from the source.** Each blocking finding is repaired from the material the text already rests on: the source spec, the code, the recorded decision. Where the source holds no answer, the finding is a real hole, and it is recorded as a question for the person. Inventing an answer is the one move the skill forbids.
4. **Read again, and close on two clean reads.** A new pair of strangers reads the repaired text. The loop ends at two consecutive reads with zero blocking findings.

The skill states the register it holds a text to, and it ships both reader prompts verbatim, ready to paste.

---

## When it fires

Any text whose clarity matters before it ships:

- a README before a push;
- a spec section after an edit;
- a decision page before it reaches the person;
- a piece of marketing copy or an article draft.

The trigger is a person asking whether a reader will understand the text. They ask it in words like these: *"audit this text"* · *"cold-read this"* · *"is this clear"* · *"will a stranger get this"*.

---

## What it can't do

- **Design review and spec-claim verification are separate passes.** A tool like [product-prover](https://github.com/happysasha18/product-prover) argues with a spec's claims and finds design holes — a missing state, a false invariant. This skill reads prose for whether a stranger understands it. Run both on a spec; they read different failures on the same page.
- **Taste and voice stay with you.** This skill holds a text to a stated register and reports where a reader stops.
- **A finding with no source answer becomes a question for you.** The skill fills no gap from imagination.

---

## Install

Claude Code required. The skill is `SKILL.md` plus the `references/` files it points at, and installing it is a copy of the folder.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/happysasha18/text-audit.git
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/text-audit
cp -R text-audit/SKILL.md text-audit/references ~/.claude/skills/text-audit/
```

Then just ask, in any project:

> *"audit this text"* · *"cold-read this README"* · *"will a stranger understand this section"*

---

## Related

- **[live-spec](https://github.com/happysasha18/live-spec)** — the pack this skill grew up inside. Its `skills/text-audit-pack/` binds this skill's loop to the pack's own paths and record home.
- **[product-prover](https://github.com/happysasha18/product-prover)** — reads a spec for design holes; this skill reads prose for comprehension.

---

=== test_reader_prompt_shape.py ===
"""The standing reader-prompt and the pages that describe it state one shape.

WHY THIS TEST EXISTS. The prompt handed to a reader who meets a text with no context lives in
`references/reader-prompt.md`. Two other places describe that same prompt: the skill's own prose,
which tells a maintainer what the reader does, and the skill's README, aimed at a person deciding
whether to install it. On 2026-07-28, inside the live-spec pack this skill was extracted from, those
three drifted: the prompt asked for four parts per stop and said "Do not guess the missing answer",
while a fourth page said a reading carries the guess the reader made. A blind reader caught the
contradiction after it had stood for two repair rounds. This test holds the three pages this skill now
ships — SKILL.md, the prompt, and the README — to the settlement: five parts, the fourth being the
reader's guess, and none of the three claiming the reader guesses nothing.

Reach: this test opens SKILL.md, references/reader-prompt.md, and README.md, and reads their prose. It
runs no script and reads no other file.
"""
import os
import re
import unittest

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
SKILL = os.path.join(ROOT, "SKILL.md")
PROMPT = os.path.join(ROOT, "references", "reader-prompt.md")
README = os.path.join(ROOT, "README.md")


def read(path):
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        return fh.read()


class TestReaderPromptShape(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_the_prompt_asks_for_five_parts(self):
        body = read(PROMPT)
        self.assertIn("write one entry with five parts", body,
                      "the reader-prompt in %s no longer states five parts" % PROMPT)

    def test_the_fourth_part_is_the_reader_s_guess(self):
        body = read(PROMPT)
        self.assertRegex(body, r"4\.\s+the guess you made in place of the missing answer",
                         "the prompt's fourth part no longer asks for the reader's guess")

    def test_the_prompt_asks_for_no_repair(self):
        body = read(PROMPT)
        self.assertIn("Do not fix anything.", body,
                      "the prompt stopped telling the reader to fix nothing")

    def test_the_skill_body_points_at_the_prompt_s_file(self):
        # The body is the reader's way in, so it names the file the prompt lives at. A body that
        # stops naming it strands the loop's second step.
        self.assertIn("references/reader-prompt.md", read(SKILL),
                      "%s no longer points at the file holding the reader-prompt" % SKILL)

    def test_no_home_still_says_the_reader_guesses_nothing(self):
        # The sentence a 2026-07-28 settlement (upstream, inside live-spec) retired. It stood here
        # after the prompt already asked for the guess, which is the drift this test exists to catch.
        stale = re.compile(r"guess(es)? no answers")
        for path in (SKILL, PROMPT, README):
            self.assertIsNone(stale.search(read(path)),
                              "%s still says the reader guesses no answers" % path)

    def test_the_skill_prose_says_the_reader_records_the_guess(self):
        for path in (SKILL, README):
            body = read(path)
            self.assertIn("writes down the guess it made in place of a missing answer", body,
                          "%s does not say the reader records its guess" % path)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

  word stands in capitals for emphasis (an acronym or code identifier passes); no sentence names a thing
  by denying its neighbour (`a spec, not a plan`, where the denied half hands the reader nothing — a
  contrast between two things the reader already holds passes); no adjective grades a result's size
  (*big*, *huge*, *minor*, *breakthrough*). Grep fallback: read for those classes by hand; the
  neighbour-denying one shows up as *not* after a comma or a dash.
- **One name per thing.** No file, script, command, or concept appears under two names. Grep fallback:
  list each named thing and confirm one name carries it throughout.

A mechanical hit is fixed before the cold reader runs, so no reader spends a finding on a class a
machine already owns. Where a text carries no spec section, the requirement-shape lint has nothing to
read; note the refusal in the reading record and move on, rather than editing the text or the lint to
force a pass.

## The cold reader

Hand the text to two fresh sessions: one under `references/reader-prompt.md`, which prints dozens of
kinds of place to stop, and one under `references/unprompted-reader-brief.md`, which prints none. Both
run on every audit. Each reader holds zero context on the text's history — no earlier draft, no
project background, no author's intent beyond the page — kept apart from anyone holding the project's
own rules.

Every finding is marked blocking or non-blocking, by one test: the reader could not go on, or would
have applied the text wrongly. Most blocking findings are an undefined term the rest of the text leans
on, a relational word whose slot decides what the reader does, or a claim with no findable ground; that
test decides any case outside them. A non-blocking finding is a place that still reads, where the fix
would only sharpen it. The loop closes when both readers of a round return zero blocking findings,
twice in a row; the non-blocking ones go to the person as a list, theirs to spend a rewrite on.

**The prompted reader** tends to catch local sentence mechanics: a pronoun with no antecedent, one word
carrying two meanings, a sentence with no actor, an image with no referent. **The unprompted reader**
opens what a claim cites, runs the steps the text teaches, and checks a number against its source; it
tends to catch whether the document can be used at all — a missing prerequisite, an install section
that installs nothing the page promises, a link to the wrong repository, a rule its own evidence
contradicts, an arithmetic error. Neither reader alone covers both classes, and the passages both
readers stop on are the strongest evidence a text has a real problem there. Running both costs more
judging work than one reader alone — expect a sizeable share of what either returns to fall away under
refutation — and that cost is what buys the coverage neither reader gets alone.

### The by-hand mode

A person working alone still needs a reader other than the author: someone who has not read the text,
holding the prompt and nothing else — no repository, no earlier draft, no chance to ask the writer a
question. By hand the reading step takes two such people, one under each brief, neither seeing the
other's list; the auditor merges the two by the steps in "The loop".

Where no such reader is at hand, the by-hand mode covers the mechanical lints through their grep
fallbacks and stops there — the cold read does not run, and the audit does not close. Say so in the
reading record rather than counting the text as read. Where one reader alone is at hand, the round
stands incomplete, the audit stays open, and the reading record says which brief went unread.

## Where a fix comes from

A fix comes from the material the text rests on, and nowhere else. A **term** gets the definition its
source gives it, at the term's first use. A **relational word** gets the reference point, the measure,
or the reason its source names, where the word stands. A **judgment word** gets its judge and its
inputs, from the source that decides the judgment. A **claim** gets its ground stated, or shrinks to
what the source supports. That material is the source spec, the code, the recorded decision, or the
author's own notes.

Sometimes the source holds no answer: the spec is silent, the decision was never made, the number was
never set. That finding is a genuine hole — record it as a question for the person, with a visible mark
at the spot, so the open question travels with the text. A spec section takes an inline
`[GAP: what is missing]` note; other texts take a bracketed query in the draft.

Inventing an answer to close a finding is the one move this skill forbids. An invented definition hides
the hole from the next reader, and leaves the text stating what no source backs.

# The rules a human-prose audit holds a text to

This file belongs to the `text-audit` skill, whose body is [`../SKILL.md`](../SKILL.md). That body
defines a surface and a register, and it says when a text is held to the rules below.

The rules below are the whole set this skill's own audit holds human prose to, as a static, hand-kept
list. They were extracted on 2026-08-18 from a fuller rule home that lives in the live-spec pack this
skill was pulled out of (`github.com/happysasha18/live-spec`), which builds several companion pages —
a writer's page with each rule's examples and thresholds, a maintainer's page, and the rule text a
judging model reads — off that one home. Adding a rule there no longer reaches this file; a host
project that wants the fuller, moving set points `.text-audit/lints.json` at its own rule home instead,
and where it does not, the rules below are the whole set this skill checks.

## The rules this audit holds human prose to

Every rule below binds human prose, which is text a person reads to understand something or to decide something. A README, a decision page, a report, a skill's own body, and a documentation page carry it. So do the prose paragraphs inside a spec. A documentation page carries `artifact` as well once it is published outside the project.

This block prints 50 of the 66 rules the source carries. A code missing from the run below belongs to a rule binding other surfaces only, or to a retired rule whose code left the set. A rule binding human prose may also bind chat, a commit message, or a worker brief. Its recorded case may come from one of those surfaces.

They are printed here out of `guardrails/language-rules.json`, which is where each one is edited. A change made in this block is overwritten by the next run of `scripts/gen-language-consumers.py`.

Each entry names the class of mistake, states the rule, gives the question to ask of a sentence, and carries one recorded case under it. The case shows written text on the left. The right side shows its repair, or an instruction where the repair depends on facts the case does not carry. Every case the class was built from lives in the rule home.

- **an ordinary word carrying a private project meaning** (`r01`)
  A word keeps its everyday meaning. A term this project needs holds one glossary entry, written in plain words. The body then uses that term unchanged, with no definition attached.
  *Ask:* Would a person outside this project recognize this word, or does the text gloss it in plain words where it first appears?
    - `The system shall red a branch whose merge-base sits behind main's tip.` → `The system shall refuse a branch whose merge-base sits behind main's tip.`
- **a coined, loan-translated, or respelled word standing where a plain standard word exists** (`r02`)
  Where the industry has a word, the text writes the industry's word. A term this project coined is replaced by the standard word, or defined where it first appears. In the reader's own language, a term is written as a real word of that language.
  *Ask:* Does a standard word already name this thing? Is the word used here that standard word, written as a real word of the reader's own language?

# Checking that a rewrite still instructs the same thing

This file belongs to the `text-audit` skill, whose body is [`../SKILL.md`](../SKILL.md). The body's
loop asks whether a stranger understands a text. This file asks a second question of a rewrite: does
the new text still tell its reader to do the same thing?

Run these steps over any rewrite of text that binds someone. A skill body, a guardrail's printed
message, a spec criterion, an installed file, and a step a reader follows all bind someone.

Why the steps exist: a rewrite of eleven skill files dropped phrases the test suite required. Nobody
read the old and the new version side by side. The audit loop in the skill body reads how the new
text lands on a stranger. It reports nothing about the eight fields in step 1.

Every path below is relative to the root of the live-spec repository, which is the directory holding
`PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, `guardrails/`, and `scripts/`. A path opening with `references/` names a file in
this skill's own directory, beside this one.

## Step 1 — put each changed unit beside the version it replaces

Take the rewrite one unit at a time. A unit is one criterion, one paragraph, or one list item. Put it
beside the text it replaces, and answer all eight questions. Write each answer on its own line.

| Field | The question to answer |
|---|---|
| Actor | Does the same person or the same part of the system act? |
| Force | Do must, should, may, and any prohibition carry the same weight? |
| Condition | Does the rule apply under the same trigger? |
| Scope | Does it bind the same text, system, people, and stretch of time? |
| Threshold | Are the quantities, units, direction, and comparison unchanged? |
| Exception | Does every carve-out and every fallback survive? |
| Output | Are the names, formats, destinations, and generated files unchanged? |
| Side effect | Does the same action change the same state? |

A change made on purpose gets its own line under the field it moved. Keep those lines apart from the
readability findings, so whoever reads the record can tell the two apart.

## Step 2 — resolve every path and run every command the text teaches

- Open every path, link, and file name the changed text carries, and confirm each one resolves.
- Run every command the text teaches, from the working directory the text names.

**text-audit** — the canonical text-audit, in its own repository with its own version line.

# text-audit

**An audit-and-fix loop for any human-facing text. It runs the mechanical lints, reads the text as a stranger, and repairs the places where the stranger stops. A [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) skill.**

Point it at a text a person will read: a README, a spec section, a decision page, marketing copy, an article. It runs the free mechanical lints first. Then it hands the text to a fresh reader who knows nothing of its history, and that reader marks every place a stranger stops. You repair those places from the source material, and a new reader reads again. The loop ends when two consecutive reads return nothing that blocks a reader.

---

## Why

The author of a text is the worst reader of it. The author already holds the context the text is missing, so the author reads a meaning a stranger cannot reach. Three examples show the shape:

- a term that was never defined;
- a phrase such as "depends on the upstream state", whose slot stands empty;
- a claim whose ground lives in the author's head.

The text reads fine to the person who wrote it, and it stops a stranger cold.

The repair is a reader who holds none of that context. This skill supplies the stranger. A fresh session reads the words on the page and reports where it stopped. Each stop is marked by whether it blocks a reader or only slows one. You repair the blocking stops from the material the text rests on, and a new stranger reads again. Two clean reads in a row show that the stream of stops has reached zero.

This skill grew inside [live-spec](https://github.com/happysasha18/live-spec), out of a comprehension gate its pipeline held every changed spec section to: a panel of fresh readers found new blocking terms on every pass, and the terms already repaired stayed repaired. It was pulled out into its own repository on 2026-08-18 so any project can run the loop, not only that one.

---

## What it does

1. **The mechanical lints first.** Five lints run before any reader:

   - a term defined at first use;
   - a weak relational word with an unfilled slot;
   - requirement shape, where the text is a spec;
   - style and register;
   - one name per thing.

   A machine settles those cheap classes, so the reader spends attention on the ones no machine knows yet. A host project may declare its own scripts for any of these in `.text-audit/lints.json`; where none is declared, a grep fallback needing no script covers the same ground.
2. **Two fresh cold readers.** The text goes to two sessions with zero context on its history: one under a printed reader-prompt, one under an unprompted brief holding only the text and the task. Both return the places a stranger stops, each marked blocking or non-blocking. Neither fixes anything, and each writes down the guess it made in place of a missing answer.
3. **Fixes from the source.** Each blocking finding is repaired from the material the text already rests on: the source spec, the code, the recorded decision. Where the source holds no answer, the finding is a real hole, and it is recorded as a question for the person. Inventing an answer is the one move the skill forbids.
4. **Read again, and close on two clean reads.** A new pair of strangers reads the repaired text. The loop ends at two consecutive reads with zero blocking findings.

The skill states the register it holds a text to, and it ships both reader prompts verbatim, ready to paste.

---

## When it fires

Any text whose clarity matters before it ships:

- a README before a push;
- a spec section after an edit;
- a decision page before it reaches the person;
- a piece of marketing copy or an article draft.

The trigger is a person asking whether a reader will understand the text. They ask it in words like these: *"audit this text"* · *"cold-read this"* · *"is this clear"* · *"will a stranger get this"*.

---

## What it can't do

- **Design review and spec-claim verification are separate passes.** A tool like [product-prover](https://github.com/happysasha18/product-prover) argues with a spec's claims and finds design holes — a missing state, a false invariant. This skill reads prose for whether a stranger understands it. Run both on a spec; they read different failures on the same page.
- **Taste and voice stay with you.** This skill holds a text to a stated register and reports where a reader stops.
- **A finding with no source answer becomes a question for you.** The skill fills no gap from imagination.

---

## Install

[Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) is required, with the Anthropic account it runs on. The skill is `SKILL.md` plus the `references/` files it points at, and installing it is a copy of the folder.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/happysasha18/text-audit.git
cd text-audit
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/text-audit
cp -R SKILL.md references ~/.claude/skills/text-audit/
ls ~/.claude/skills/text-audit
# SKILL.md   references
```

Claude Code picks up skills placed in `~/.claude/skills/` automatically; open a new session if one was already running. Then ask, in any project:

> *"audit this text"* · *"cold-read this README"* · *"is this clear"* · *"will a stranger understand this section"*

---

## What proves it

The three files under [`evals/fixtures/text-audit/`](evals/fixtures/text-audit/) are planted-defect texts: each carries one known comprehension defect on purpose. `ambiguous-explanation.md` leaves three relational words' slots unfilled ("some time", "an appropriate stretch", "quickly"). `rewrite-weakens-the-rule.md` pairs a rule with a rewrite that quietly changes its actor, softens its force, and drops its exception. `clean-prose-wrong-command.md` reads clean while teaching a command that fails. [`references/rewrite-meaning-check.md`](references/rewrite-meaning-check.md) is the checklist that walks a rewrite against the version it replaces; its own text points at these three fixtures as the check on any worker that claims to run it.

---

## Related

- **[live-spec](https://github.com/happysasha18/live-spec)** — the pack this skill grew up inside. Its `skills/text-audit-pack/` binds this skill's loop to the pack's own paths and record home.
- **[product-prover](https://github.com/happysasha18/product-prover)** — reads a spec for design holes; this skill reads prose for comprehension.

---

[MIT](LICENSE) © Alexander Abramovich. The skill is prose, so it pulls in no third-party code and carries no dependency of its own. This is release `1.0.0`, and this repository's version line is the only one the skill follows.

---

## Release history

See [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md).

readings returned nothing that blocked. That gate is where the five-step loop this skill runs came
from.

On 2026-08-18 the skill was pulled out of that pack into this repository, the same move
[product-prover](https://github.com/happysasha18/product-prover) made earlier from the same pack. The
pack's own review of the move (recorded in its history as
`docs/skill-review/2026-08-18-text-audit-extraction.md`) verified the removal was clean: no dangling
pin, no generator left writing into a path that no longer exists, no roster still claiming the skill's
body lives in that tree. In its place the pack now keeps a thin adapter,
`skills/text-audit-pack/`, that binds this skill's loop to the pack's own paths and record home.

**This repository is now the canon.** `SKILL.md` and `references/` version here first; the pack's
adapter follows this repository rather than the other way around. This repository's own version line
starts at `1.0.0`, independent of whatever version number the pack's shared release cycle carries.

Two files this skill ships were, before the move, generated on every build from a fuller rule home the
pack keeps: `references/reader-prompt.md` and `references/human-prose-rules.md`. Both say so in their
own text. They are now static, hand-kept copies: no generator owns them here, and a change to either
is versioned like any other change to this repository. A host project that wants the pack's fuller,
moving rule set can point its own `.text-audit/lints.json` at it instead of relying on the copies this
repository ships.

requirements document — nothing here needed resolving into plain words before it could ship on its
own. The `[INV-241]`-style bracket anchor named in `SKILL.md` and in the sample fixtures is an example
of a citation *inside an audited document*, not a citation this skill's own instructions depend on.

# Provenance

This skill grew inside [live-spec](https://github.com/happysasha18/live-spec), a pipeline that takes a
product spec from a wish through to shipped code. Its comprehension gate held every changed spec
section to a fresh-reader pass before the section could ship: a panel of readers holding no context on
the section's history reported where they stopped, and the section did not pass until two consecutive
readings returned nothing that blocked. That gate is where the five-step loop this skill runs came
from.

On 2026-08-18 the skill was pulled out of that pack into this repository, the same move
[product-prover](https://github.com/happysasha18/product-prover) made earlier from the same pack. The
pack's own review of the move (recorded in its history as
`docs/skill-review/2026-08-18-text-audit-extraction.md`) verified the removal was clean: no dangling
pin, no generator left writing into a path that no longer exists, no roster still claiming the skill's
body lives in that tree. In its place the pack now keeps a thin adapter,
`skills/text-audit-pack/`, that binds this skill's loop to the pack's own paths and record home.

**This repository is now the canon.** `SKILL.md` and `references/` version here first; the pack's
adapter follows this repository rather than the other way around. This repository's own version line
starts at `1.0.0`, independent of whatever version number the pack's shared release cycle carries.

Two files this skill ships were, before the move, generated on every build from a fuller rule home the
pack keeps: `references/reader-prompt.md` and `references/human-prose-rules.md`. Both say so in their
own text. They are now static, hand-kept copies: no generator owns them here, and a change to either
is versioned like any other change to this repository. A host project that wants the pack's fuller,
moving rule set can point its own `.text-audit/lints.json` at it instead of relying on the copies this
repository ships.

Unlike product-prover, this skill's own text carries no internal rule codes standing in for a private
requirements document — nothing here needed resolving into plain words before it could ship on its
own. The `[INV-241]`-style bracket anchor named in `SKILL.md` and in the sample fixtures is an example
of a citation *inside an audited document*, not a citation this skill's own instructions depend on.

# Checking that a rewrite still instructs the same thing

This file belongs to the `text-audit` skill, whose body is [`../SKILL.md`](../SKILL.md). The body's
loop asks whether a stranger understands a text. This file asks a second question of a rewrite: does
the new text still tell its reader to do the same thing?

Run these steps over any rewrite of text that binds someone. A skill body, a guardrail's printed
message, a spec criterion, an installed file, and a step a reader follows all bind someone.

Why the steps exist: a rewrite of eleven skill files dropped phrases the test suite required. Nobody
read the old and the new version side by side. The audit loop in the skill body reads how the new
text lands on a stranger. It reports nothing about the eight fields in step 1.

Every path below is relative to the root of the live-spec repository, which is the directory holding
`PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, `guardrails/`, and `scripts/`. A path opening with `references/` names a file in
this skill's own directory, beside this one.

## Step 1 — put each changed unit beside the version it replaces

Take the rewrite one unit at a time. A unit is one criterion, one paragraph, or one list item. Put it
beside the text it replaces, and answer all eight questions. Write each answer on its own line.

| Field | The question to answer |
|---|---|
| Actor | Does the same person or the same part of the system act? |
| Force | Do must, should, may, and any prohibition carry the same weight? |
| Condition | Does the rule apply under the same trigger? |
| Scope | Does it bind the same text, system, people, and stretch of time? |
| Threshold | Are the quantities, units, direction, and comparison unchanged? |
| Exception | Does every carve-out and every fallback survive? |

readability findings, so whoever reads the record can tell the two apart.

## Step 2 — resolve every path and run every command the text teaches

- Open every path, link, and file name the changed text carries, and confirm each one resolves.
- Run every command the text teaches, from the working directory the text names.
- Carry out each taught step in a temporary directory, and read what it produced.
- Run the suite from the repository root: `python3 -m pytest -q`.

The suite pins exact phrases out of these documents, so a dropped phrase turns a test red. When a test
fails on a phrase, say which of three kinds that phrase is:

- the phrase carries the rule, so the rewrite changed the rule and the rewrite goes back;
- the phrase names something another file depends on, so both move in one change;
- the phrase is incidental wording, and the test may take the new words.

A test takes new words only in the third case.

## Step 3 — edit the source of a generated file, then regenerate

Find the source and the generator before touching anything. `scripts/gen-language-consumers.py` builds
four files out of `guardrails/language-rules.json`:

A hand edit to any of them turns `python3 guardrails/check-language-rules.py` red. Edit the source, run
the generator, and compare every one of those files against a fresh build.

PRODUCT_SPEC.index.md`.

## Step 4 — install into a temporary home and compare

## Step 6 — hold the recorded finding count

Where a host project tracks a findings budget per file — how many style- and register-lint hits, and
how many sentences past the 25-word human-prose cap, a file is allowed to carry before a push is
refused — record that count the first time a file is measured, and treat any rise above the recorded

content.content:
# Checking that a rewrite still instructs the same thing

This file belongs to the `text-audit` skill, whose body is [`../SKILL.md`](../SKILL.md). The body's
loop asks whether a stranger understands a text. This file asks a second question of a rewrite: does
the new text still tell its reader to do the same thing?

Run these steps over any rewrite of text that binds someone. A skill body, a guardrail's printed
message, a spec criterion, an installed file, and a step a reader follows all bind someone.

Why the steps exist: a rewrite of eleven skill files dropped phrases the test suite required. Nobody
read the old and the new version side by side. The audit loop in the skill body reads how the new
text lands on a stranger. It reports nothing about the eight fields in step 1.

A path opening with `references/` or `evals/` below names a file in this repository, beside this one.
Any other path belongs to whichever pack or host project a step is written for, and is named at that
point rather than assumed to be on your disk.

## Step 1 — put each changed unit beside the version it replaces

Take the rewrite one unit at a time. A unit is one criterion, one paragraph, or one list item. Put it
beside the text it replaces, and answer all eight questions. Write each answer on its own line.

| Field | The question to answer |
|---|---|
| Actor | Does the same person or the same part of the system act? |
| Force | Do must, should, may, and any prohibition carry the same weight? |
| Condition | Does the rule apply under the same trigger? |
| Scope | Does it bind the same text, system, people, and stretch of time? |
| Threshold | Are the quantities, units, direction, and comparison unchanged? |
| Exception | Does every carve-out and every fallback survive? |
| Output | Are the names, formats, destinations, and generated files unchanged? |
| Side effect | Does the same action change the same state? |

A change made on purpose gets its own line under the field it moved. Keep those lines apart from the
readability findings, so whoever reads the record can tell the two apart.

## Step 2 — resolve every path and run every command the text teaches

- Open every path, link, and file name the changed text carries, and confirm each one resolves.
- Run every command the text teaches, from the working directory the text names.
- Carry out each taught step in a temporary directory, and read what it produced.
- Run the suite from the repository root: `python3 -m pytest -q`.

The suite pins exact phrases out of these documents, so a dropped phrase turns a test red. When a test
fails on a phrase, say which of three kinds that phrase is:

- the phrase carries the rule, so the rewrite changed the rule and the rewrite goes back;
- the phrase names something another file depends on, so both move in one change;
- the phrase is incidental wording, and the test may take the new words.

A test takes new words only in the third case.

## Step 3 — edit the source of a generated file, then regenerate

Find the source and the generator before touching anything. Where a text is a generated file — built by
a script from a source of record, rather than edited by hand — a hand edit to the generated copy either
gets silently overwritten or drifts from its source.
[`references/reader-prompt.md`](reader-prompt.md) and [`references/human-prose-rules.md`](human-prose-rules.md)
in this repository are static, hand-kept copies with no generator of their own (see `PROVENANCE.md`); a
host project that keeps its own fuller rule home behind `.text-audit/lints.json` may still generate its
consumers from it, and that generator is where the edit belongs, not the file it writes.

Edit the source, run the generator, and compare every file it builds against a fresh build. Send the
generator to a scratch directory rather than the project's own tree, so a fresh build can be read
without writing over anything still under review.

## Step 4 — install into a temporary home and compare

Run this repository's own install commands (see README's Install section) into a throwaway home, so a
live copy on the machine stays untouched:

```bash
tmp_home="$(mktemp -d)"
mkdir -p "$tmp_home/.claude/skills/text-audit"
cp -R SKILL.md references "$tmp_home/.claude/skills/text-audit/"
diff -r references "$tmp_home/.claude/skills/text-audit/references"
```

The copy carries the reference files as well, so a reference the rewrite added shows up in the diff.

## Step 5 — report what a session pays to read the rewrite

Give the sizes separately, so whoever reads the report can see where the words went:

```bash
wc -c SKILL.md references/*.md
```

The frontmatter at the top of `SKILL.md` is indexed in every session. The body loads when the skill
loads. Each file under `references/` loads only for the task that needs it.

## Step 6 — hold the recorded finding count

Where a host project tracks a findings budget per file — how many style- and register-lint hits, and
how many sentences past the 25-word human-prose cap, a file is allowed to carry before a push is
refused — record that count the first time a file is measured, and treat any rise above the recorded
count as a break. A file recorded at zero reds on its first finding. A file the record has never heard
of also reds, so a new file is measured and recorded before it can pass.

## The texts that prove a step catches something

`evals/fixtures/text-audit/` holds three short texts, each carrying one known defect. The test
`tests/test_text_audit_fixtures.py` names the planted defect of each one, and it says which shipped
check reports that defect.

Hand `evals/fixtures/text-audit/rewrite-weakens-the-rule.md` to any worker that claims to verify a
rewrite. A worker that misses the changed actor, the softened force, or the dropped exception has
failed before it touches a real document.
